newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel minister withdraws budget cut proposal.
newsitem.headline: Israel minister withdraws budget cut proposal.

text.p: Israeli Finance Minister Yaacov Neeman on Sunday withdrew from the parliamentary finance committee a proposal to cut the 1997 budget by 800 million shekels ($227 million), parliamentary officials said.
Neeman withdrew the proposal at the last minute when it became clear it was not going to pass. The cut has already been approved by the cabinet
Officials said he plannec to reintroduce at a later date.

"The finance minister needs to do some soul-searching with regard to his relationship with the Knesset (parliament) finance committee and learn what to pass and how," said committee member Ophir Pines of the Labour party.
Members of Shas and the National Religious Party, both coalition parties, said they opposed any attempt to cut the education and social welfare budgets.
"If coalition members won't support the government then I have nothing to do here," Neeman told reporters.
Separately, Neeman told the cabinet that the inflation target in 1998 would remain at the 1997 level of seven to 10 percent, ministry officials said.

The cabinet met on Sunday to discuss the 1998 budget and the Treasury's proposal for structural reforms, aimed at reviving growth next year. No decisions were taken and the cabinet will reconvene on Monday.
Neeman told reporters after the meeting that he had fixed a "realistic" target for next year.
"If I were to fix an impossible target that would be as if I couldn't see the reality," Neeman said.
The Bank of Israel favours lowering the inflation target in 1998.
Neeman said inflation this year was running at 9.5 to 10 percent, at the upper end of the 1997 target. Lowering the target next year would increase unemployment, already on the rise, he added.
The Finance Ministry also said it had agreed to the Agriculture Ministry's request not to lift all restrictions on the import of agricultural goods, as called for by the proposal.
The two ministries agreed however to lift restrictions on imports of hard cheese.
The Treasury's economic plan, unveiled on Thursday, includes measures for privatisation, capital market reform and foreign currency liberalisation.

"The structural changes will increase the competition and efficiency in the economy and improve the profits for all Israeli citizens," Finance Ministry director general Shmuel Slavin told the cabinet.
"Non-implementation of the steps presented here will lead to an economic standstill with an increase in unemployment up to some 11 percent," he said.
Unemployment was 7.3 percent in the first quarter of 1997.
The Histadrut labour federation has threatened action if recommendations on privatisation and increased competition in industries dominated by government companies are approved.
"Strikes are to the detriment of the workers. If, heaven forbid, there will be an unjust strike I will seriously consider the issue," Neeman said.
For 1998 the Treasury has set a budget of 164.4 billion shekels. From this it proposes to cut about 2.5 billion shekels.
It is asking the cabinet to set next year's budget deficit at 8.5 billion shekels or 2.4 percent of gross domestic product.
The cabinet will meet on August 31 to vote on the budget before sending it to parliament for approval by year end.
($1 = 3.53 shekels)
